passage:
Dear Maa,
You asked about your grandson. Divyansh is fourteen now and has discovered grunting. Last Sunday he spent six hours at his desk with online classes and then his phone, and by evening he snapped at everyone, slammed his door and called dinner "disgusting".
My first instinct was to lecture him. Instead I remembered how Papa used to take me cycling when I was cross. So I knocked and said, "I'm going to the lake for a walk. Come with me? No talking required." He shrugged, but he came.
We walked for half an hour, mostly in silence. Halfway round he started telling me about a friend who's upset with him. When we got home, he actually ate. We've gone three evenings this week, and I never once had to ask what was wrong.
Love,
Alka

qa.q: Where did Alka invite Divyansh to walk?
qa.a: Alka invited Divyansh to walk to the lake.

qa.q: What was Alka tempted to do when Divyansh snapped, and what does that show about Alka's feelings?
qa.a: Alka's first instinct was to lecture, which shows frustration, but Alka chose a walk instead.

qa.q: Why did inviting Divyansh as company work better than an order?
qa.a: "Come with me? No talking required" felt like company, not a punishment, so Divyansh came and opened up while moving.

qa.q: What might the walk have felt like for Divyansh?
qa.a: Divyansh may have felt relieved to move after hours at a desk and free to talk without pressure.

grounding: A parent notices a teen snappy after long hours at a desk and phone, and offers a walk as company that lifts his mood without a talk.

passage:
My son Nilesh is sixteen, and during the holidays he turned into a sort of cave creature. Curtains shut, laptop, phone, back to laptop. By evening he'd be jumpy and rude, and I'd be rude back. Once I said, "Get out and exercise, you're rotting!" He slammed the door. Obviously.
Then I tried something else. I dusted off my old cycle and said, "I'm riding to the bakery for pav. The hill kills me. Will you come and push me up it?" He laughed, the first laugh in days, and came. We rode for twenty minutes. He raced ahead, came back, raced ahead again. At home he was a different boy, chatty even. Now it's our evening thing. I'm Nandini, by the way, and I never once had to ask him what was wrong.

qa.q: Where was Nandini riding to?
qa.a: Nandini was riding to the bakery for pav.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling during those holiday evenings?
qa.a: Nandini felt frustrated and worn down, becoming rude back when Nilesh was jumpy.

qa.q: What went wrong with the first approach, and what worked?
qa.a: The order to exercise sounded like an insult and got a slammed door; inviting Nilesh along as company on a ride worked.

qa.q: What might the ride have been like for Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh likely enjoyed the chance to move and laugh, racing ahead and coming back, without feeling lectured.

grounding: A parent sees a teen jumpy after hours on screens and finds that movement offered as company lifts his mood better than an order.

passage: I'm Suraj, Payal's father, and I'll tell you what I saw last Sunday, though I can't say for sure what was going on inside her. She'd been at her desk since breakfast, online class, then homework, then her phone. By four, she was snapping at everyone. Her mother asked about lunch and got a sharp 'I don't care!' The door banged. I didn't lecture. I knocked and said, 'I'm going to cycle to the lake to buy corn. Want to come? You can ride ahead.' She shrugged, but came. For the first ten minutes she didn't say a word. Then, by the lake, she laughed at a dog chasing ducks. On the way back she told me about a friend's joke. I don't know if it was the air, the cycling or just not being told off. But she was different.

qa.q: What did Suraj go to the lake to buy?
qa.a: Corn.

qa.q: What might Suraj have been feeling when he chose not to lecture?
qa.a: Suraj seems calm and caring, wanting to help rather than scold, even without knowing what was wrong.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Payal on a ride as company, not an order, gave her movement and space without pressure to talk.

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced the ride?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved to get out of the room without being told off, and slowly lighter as she moved.

grounding: Shows, through a parent's account, a teenager snappy after hours at a desk and phone, and a cycling invitation offered as company that lifts her mood.

passage:
Friday: After six hours of online classes and gaming, Nitin snapped at Amandeep over nothing and slammed his laptop shut. Amandeep, his mother, shouted back and he stormed off.
Saturday: He was hunched at the desk again by noon. 'Go out for a walk, you've been sitting all day!' she ordered. 'Stop telling me what to do!' he yelled. It was worse.
Sunday: Amandeep tried something different. She picked up the shopping bag. 'I'm walking to the vegetable market. Come keep me company?' Nitin grumbled but came. They walked twenty minutes, mostly silent. On the way back, he offered to carry the bag and started talking about a new game. At home he was calm all evening.

qa.q: How many hours of online classes and gaming had Nitin done on Friday?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she tried something different on Sunday?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated after two bad days but hopeful that a gentler invitation might work.

qa.q: What was the difference between Saturday and Sunday?
qa.a: On Saturday the walk was an order and made things worse; on Sunday it was an invitation for company, and it helped.

qa.q: How might Nitin have experienced his mother's Sunday invitation?
qa.a: He probably felt less controlled and more wanted, which made it easier to join and relax.

grounding: Shows a parent who sees a teenager snappy after long sitting and learns that movement works better when offered as company, not as an order.

passage: Kiran, you're sighing like the whole world is against you. Let your Sachin Dada tell you something about your Papa. When he was sixteen, before his board exams, he sat at that same desk from morning till night. By evening he'd bite anyone's head off. Your Dadi would scold, and he'd shout, and the whole house would be on fire. I had no clever words. So one evening I just wheeled out my old cycle and said, 'I'm going to the lake. Coming?' He grumbled but came. We didn't talk much. We cycled round the lake twice, watched the boats, and came back. He was a different boy. After that, every evening we cycled. No lectures, just company. He passed, and he still calls those rides the best part of that year.

qa.q: Where did Sachin and his son cycle?
qa.a: Round the lake.

qa.q: How did Kiran's Papa feel after long days at the desk?
qa.a: He was irritable and snappy, biting anyone's head off.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sachin's story?
qa.a: Sachin stopped scolding and simply invited his son on a cycle ride as company.

qa.q: How might Kiran's Dadi have seen the evening rides?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved that the house was calmer and the shouting had stopped.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a parent who notices a teenager snappy after long hours studying and offers cycling as company, which lifts his mood.

passage: It had rained for four days in Pune, and Chinmay had spent the whole Sunday hunched over his desk and phone. By evening he snapped at his little brother, slammed his book and groaned at every question. His mother, Avni, noticed his jiggling knee and the way he kept rubbing his neck. She didn't lecture. When the rain paused around six, she tied her shoes and said, 'I'm walking to the lake before it starts again. Come keep me company?' He rolled his eyes, but came. They walked fast, dodging puddles, hardly talking. By the time they reached the bhel stall, he was joking about the frogs. The rain came back on the way home, and they ran the last stretch, laughing.

qa.q: Where did Avni say she was walking?
qa.a: To the lake, before the rain started again.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she saw Chinmay's jiggling knee?
qa.a: Avni felt concerned, sensing that hours of sitting had made him restless and snappy.

qa.q: Why did Avni's invitation work better than an order?
qa.a: Offering the walk as company, not a command, let Chinmay join without losing face, and the movement lifted his mood.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel by the time they reached the bhel stall?
qa.a: He felt lighter and cheerful, joking about the frogs.

grounding: A parent sees a teenager snappy after long sitting and offers a walk as company, and movement lifts his mood.
